title: Personalised Learning and Early Warning
answer: Personalised learning and early warning covers systems that adapt course material to an individual learner and systems that flag when a learner is falling behind or at risk of dropping out. In course design and teaching, the two are usually discussed together because the same student data that drives adaptation also drives the alert. The scope runs from simple rule based triggers, such as a missed deadline, to models that estimate the probability a student will fail or leave. It sits at the meeting point of instructional design, learning analytics and student support services.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Personalised learning and early warning covers systems that adapt course material to an individual learner and systems that flag when a learner is falling behind or at risk of dropping out. In course design and teaching, the two are usually discussed together because the same student data that drives adaptation also drives the alert. The scope runs from simple rule based triggers, such as a missed deadline, to models that estimate the probability a student will fail or leave. It sits at the meeting point of instructional design, learning analytics and student support services.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These systems run on the data a course already produces: grades, submission times, logins to a learning management system, forum activity, quiz attempts and attendance. That data is stored in a student record system or a learning analytics warehouse, and the models are usually trained and served from a cloud platform. A dashboard or an email alert is the common delivery surface for staff, and a recommendation panel or adaptive quiz is the common surface for students. Institutional identity and access management controls who sees which student record.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with defining the outcome to predict or the learning goal to adapt to, then choosing features that are available early enough to be useful. Early warning models are typically trained on historical cohorts with a labelled outcome such as pass, fail or withdrawal, and validated on a later cohort rather than a random split. Personalised learning uses the same signals to select content, pace or practice items, often through knowledge tracing or recommender methods. Both need a baseline comparison, because a simple rule about missed submissions is hard to beat and easy to explain.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Student data is sensitive, and the legal basis for processing it varies by jurisdiction, so most institutions route these projects through a data protection review and an ethics committee. Provenance matters in two directions: the source of each data field should be documented, and any research claim about a model's accuracy should trace to the original paper rather than a summary. Risk includes labelling a student as likely to fail, which can become self fulfilling if the label reaches the student or shapes staff expectations. Access should be limited to staff with a support role, and students should be able to see and contest what is recorded about them.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward models that explain their alerts in plain language and toward support actions tied to each flag, rather than dashboards that only display risk scores. There is growing interest in adapting to the learner's own goals and in measuring whether an intervention actually helped, not just whether the prediction was accurate. Work on fairness across student groups is becoming a standard part of evaluation. The open question is whether these systems improve outcomes or mainly make existing disadvantage more visible.
